questions.stem: A client with sepsis develops acute dyspnea. The chest x-ray shows bilateral infiltrates without cardiomegaly, the PaO2/FiO2 ratio is 180, and hypoxemia persists despite rising oxygen delivery. No cardiac cause is found. Which condition should the nurse suspect?
options: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema from heart failure
Acute respiratory distress syndrome
Tension pneumothorax on the affected side
Acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis
rationales: Incorrect. The book describes ARDS as noncardiogenic edema; here no cardiac cause and no cardiomegaly were found.
Correct. Acute onset, bilateral infiltrates, a PaO2/FiO2 ratio under 300, refractory hypoxemia and no cardiac cause point to ARDS.
Incorrect. Tension pneumothorax shows tracheal deviation, distended neck veins and hypotension, not diffuse bilateral infiltrates.
Incorrect. A COPD exacerbation worsens chronic symptoms; it does not explain new bilateral infiltrates with refractory hypoxemia.
questions.clue: Bilateral infiltrates, PaO2/FiO2 below 300 and no cardiac cause.
questions.priority: Recognize ARDS early from its defining criteria.

questions.stem: A client with ARDS on mechanical ventilation with high PEEP becomes hypotensive. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Discontinue PEEP until the blood pressure recovers
Silence the ventilator alarms to reduce stimulation
Raise the tidal volume to improve cardiac output
Treat the hypotension as ordered while keeping PEEP in place
rationales: Incorrect. Stopping PEEP lets alveoli collapse and worsens oxygenation; the book says do not discontinue it.
Incorrect. The book states ventilator alarms should never be set to the off position.
Incorrect. Tidal volume is limited to 4 to 8 mL/kg to prevent volutrauma, and raising it does not treat hypotension.
Correct. The book states to treat hypotension and not discontinue PEEP, which is needed to keep alveoli open.
questions.clue: Hypotension develops in a client receiving high PEEP.
questions.priority: Maintain oxygenation support while managing reduced cardiac output.

questions.stem: A ventilated client with moderate to severe ARDS has a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 120. Which plan of care is consistent with evidence-based ARDS treatment?
options: Prone positioning with tidal volume 4 to 8 mL/kg of ideal weight
Routine corticosteroids for this non-COVID-19 ARDS
A liberal fluid strategy to support lung perfusion
Larger tidal volumes to bring the PaCO2 back to normal
rationales: Correct. The book lists low tidal volume ventilation and prone positioning for ratios under 150 as treatments that lower mortality.
Incorrect. The book says to avoid routine corticosteroids unless the ARDS is related to COVID-19.
Incorrect. The book recommends a fluid-conservative strategy to improve lung function and ventilator-free days.
Incorrect. Permissive hypercapnia is accepted; large volumes raise the risk of barotrauma and volutrauma.
questions.clue: PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 120 indicates moderate to severe ARDS.
questions.priority: Apply lung-protective ventilation and positioning.

questions.stem: A client with severe ARDS who is difficult to ventilate because of poor gas exchange is started on a continuous vecuronium infusion. Which statements about this therapy are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: It sedates the client, so a separate sedative is not needed
It must always be given together with analgesics and sedatives
It increases chest wall compliance
It is a routine first-line drug for every client with mild ARDS
It reduces the client's work of breathing
rationales: Incorrect. Neuromuscular blocking agents paralyze skeletal muscle; the book says they are always given with analgesics and sedatives for comfort and safety.
Correct. The book states neuromuscular blocking agents are always administered with analgesics and sedatives.
Correct. The book lists increased chest wall compliance as an effect of neuromuscular blocking agents.
Incorrect. The book describes use in clients who are difficult to ventilate because of poor gas exchange, not routine use in mild disease.
Correct. The book states these agents reduce the work of breathing.
questions.clue: A client who is difficult to ventilate is paralyzed with vecuronium.
questions.priority: Give neuromuscular blockade safely, with analgesia and sedation.

questions.stem: A client with worsening ARDS is being considered for BiPAP. For each finding, indicate whether it is a contraindication to BiPAP/CPAP.
rationales: Copious secretions are listed as a contraindication to BiPAP/CPAP.
Hemodynamic instability is listed as a contraindication to BiPAP/CPAP.
Being alert is not a listed contraindication; it is altered level of consciousness (ALOC) that is listed.
A high risk of aspiration is listed as a contraindication to BiPAP/CPAP.
ALOC is listed as a contraindication to BiPAP/CPAP.
questions.clue: Secretions, hemodynamics, aspiration risk and level of consciousness.
questions.priority: Screen for contraindications before noninvasive ventilation.

questions.stem: The nurse enters the room of a ventilated client with ARDS and finds that the ventilator alarms were turned off to reduce noise. What should the nurse do?
options: Leave the alarms off while staff are in the room
Turn the alarms back on and keep them active
Turn the alarms back on only at the next shift change
Leave the alarms off because the client is sedated
rationales: Incorrect. The book states ventilator alarm controls should never be set to the off position.
Correct. The book states ventilator alarm controls should never be set to the off position.
Incorrect. Waiting leaves the client unprotected; alarms must never be off.
Incorrect. Sedation does not change the rule; a sedated client cannot signal distress, and alarms must stay on.
questions.clue: Ventilator alarms are found turned off.
questions.priority: Keep ventilator alarms active at all times.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four ventilated clients with ARDS. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client receiving propofol who is sedated and resting quietly
A client on a vecuronium infusion with analgesia and sedation running
A client on high PEEP whose blood pressure dropped from 118/70 to 84/50
A client whose chest x-ray shows the same bilateral ground-glass pattern as yesterday
rationales: Incorrect. Propofol is used for continuous sedation, so a sedated, resting client is the expected response.
Incorrect. The book says neuromuscular blockers are always given with analgesics and sedatives, so this setup is appropriate.
Correct. The book warns that PEEP can decrease cardiac output and says to treat hypotension; a new drop in blood pressure needs immediate assessment.
Incorrect. A bilateral white-out or ground-glass appearance is a typical ARDS finding, and it is unchanged.
questions.clue: A new drop in blood pressure in a client on high PEEP.
questions.priority: See the client with a new, unexpected change first.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the histories of several clients in a step-down unit. Which conditions does the nurse recognize as causes of ARDS? Select all that apply.
options: Acute pancreatitis
Seasonal allergic rhinitis
Massive blood transfusion
Near drowning
Well-controlled hypothyroidism
Sepsis
rationales: Correct. Pancreatitis is shown among the indirect lung injuries that cause ARDS.
Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis is not among the direct or indirect causes the book lists.
Correct. Massive transfusion is shown among the indirect lung injuries that cause ARDS.
Correct. Near drowning is shown among the direct lung injuries that cause ARDS.
Incorrect. Hypothyroidism is not among the causes the book lists.
Correct. The book states most cases of ARDS are linked to pneumonia and sepsis.
questions.clue: Direct and indirect lung injuries in the clients' histories.
questions.priority: Identify clients at risk for ARDS so it is recognized early.

questions.stem: Two days after hip replacement surgery, a client reports sudden shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain. The client is tachycardic and anxious. What should the nurse do first?
options: Send the client for a venous Doppler of the legs
Help the client walk in the hall to relieve the pain
Assess airway, breathing, circulation and oxygen saturation
Give the first oral dose of warfarin from home supply
rationales: Incorrect. Doppler helps find the clot source, but it comes after the client's ABCs are assessed and supported.
Incorrect. Early ambulation prevents VTE, but it is unsafe in a client with acute symptoms of a possible PE.
Correct. The book makes ABCs the first priority in any pulmonary-compromised client, especially with suspected PE.
Incorrect. Anticoagulation needs an order and diagnosis; assessing ABCs comes first.
questions.clue: Sudden dyspnea and pleuritic pain after hip surgery, a strong VTE risk.
questions.priority: Assess and support ABCs before diagnostic steps.

questions.stem: A client with a confirmed massive pulmonary embolism is hypotensive and has a low risk of bleeding. Which treatment should the nurse anticipate?
options: Oral factor Xa inhibitor with outpatient follow-up
Immediate thoracotomy before any drug therapy
Thrombolytic therapy such as alteplase
Loop diuretic alone to reduce right heart strain
rationales: Incorrect. Oral factor Xa inhibitors are described for asymptomatic PE, not a hemodynamically unstable massive PE.
Incorrect. Thoracotomy is listed only for nonresponders when catheter thrombus removal fails.
Correct. The book reserves thrombolytics for massive PE with hypotension and low bleeding risk.
Incorrect. Diuretics are supportive only; the clot itself must be broken down in an unstable client.
questions.clue: Massive PE with hypotension and low bleeding risk.
questions.priority: Restore perfusion in a hemodynamically unstable PE.

questions.stem: A client with PE is receiving a continuous heparin infusion. Which nursing intervention is most appropriate?
options: Monitor for bleeding and limit venipunctures and injections
Keep the client on strict bed rest without range of motion
Restrict oral fluids to less than 1 liter per day
Give pain medication by intramuscular injection
rationales: Correct. During anticoagulant therapy the book directs monitoring for bleeding and limiting invasive procedures.
Incorrect. The book encourages early ambulation or chair rest and range-of-motion exercises every 8 hours.
Incorrect. The book recommends at least 2 L/day of fluid if not restricted.
Incorrect. Injections are limited during anticoagulation because of the bleeding risk.
questions.clue: Client is receiving a continuous heparin infusion.
questions.priority: Prevent and detect bleeding during anticoagulation.

questions.stem: The nurse is screening hospitalized clients for venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk. Which findings does the book classify as strong risk factors? Select all that apply.
options: Oral contraceptive use
Hip replacement surgery two days ago
Spinal cord injury
Pregnancy
Fracture of the femur
Atrial fibrillation
rationales: Incorrect. The book lists oral contraceptive use as a moderate, not strong, risk factor.
Correct. Hip or knee replacement surgery is listed as a strong risk factor.
Correct. Spinal cord injury is listed as a strong risk factor.
Incorrect. The book lists pregnancy as a moderate risk factor.
Correct. Fractures of long bones such as the hip or leg are listed as a strong risk factor.
Incorrect. The book lists atrial fibrillation as a moderate risk factor.
questions.clue: Orthopedic surgery, spinal cord injury and long-bone fracture.
questions.priority: Identify clients at highest VTE risk for prevention.

questions.stem: A client is being evaluated for pulmonary embolism. For each finding, indicate whether the book lists it as a feature of massive PE or as a typical finding of most PEs.
rows: Neck vein distention with an enlarged liver
rationales: Hypotension and cold or mottled skin are shock indicators listed under massive PE.
Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain and tachypnea are respiratory findings of most PEs.
Neck vein distention and right heart failure signs are cardiac strain findings of massive PE.
A transient pleural friction rub is listed with most PEs.
Confusion and decreased consciousness are neurologic symptoms of massive PE.
questions.clue: Shock, cardiac strain and neurologic signs versus respiratory findings.
questions.priority: Distinguish massive PE, a medical emergency, from typical PE.

questions.stem: A hemodynamically stable client with PE has no fluid restriction. Which independent nursing interventions should the nurse include in the plan? Select all that apply.
options: Restrict oral fluids to less than 1 L/day
Perform active or passive ROM exercises every 8 hours
Apply compression boots to promote venous return
Keep the client on strict bed rest
Encourage at least 2 L of fluid per day
Assist with early ambulation or chair rest
rationales: Incorrect. The book recommends hydration of at least 2 L/day when fluids are not restricted.
Correct. The book lists active/passive ROM every 8 hours.
Correct. The book lists compression boots to promote venous return.
Incorrect. The book encourages early ambulation or chair rest, even for intubated clients.
Correct. The book lists hydration of 2 L/day or more if not restricted.
Correct. The book lists early ambulation or chair rest.
questions.clue: Stable client with no fluid restriction.
questions.priority: Promote venous return and prevent new clots.

questions.stem: A client newly diagnosed with PE says, "I'm scared. Nobody has told me what is wrong or what all these tests are for." Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "Try not to worry. The doctors know what they are doing."
"You need to rest now rather than ask so many questions."
"I will ask the provider for something to help you sleep."
"Tell me what worries you most, and I will explain your diagnosis and each test."
rationales: Incorrect. False reassurance dismisses the client's fear; the book says to encourage expression of fears and concerns.
Incorrect. This blocks communication; the book calls for explaining the diagnosis and all procedures and tests.
Incorrect. Medicating does not address the client's need for information and for voicing concerns.
Correct. The book's education points are to encourage expression of fears and concerns and to explain the diagnosis, prognosis and all procedures and tests.
questions.clue: The client is frightened and has not been told about the diagnosis or tests.
questions.priority: Encourage expression of fears and give clear explanations.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old client is hospitalized for treatment of a pulmonary embolism. Which nursing action best supports the child's developmental and emotional needs?
options: Provide age-appropriate play and monitor growth and development
Discourage the child from talking about worries to avoid upset
Keep all explanations of the illness from the child
Limit activities to watching television alone in the room
rationales: Correct. For children, the book directs the nurse to monitor growth and development and provide age-appropriate play.
Incorrect. The book says to encourage expression of fears and concerns.
Incorrect. The book calls for explaining the diagnosis and procedures; withholding all information is not supported.
Incorrect. Isolating the child does not meet the book's call for age-appropriate play.
questions.clue: A school-age child is hospitalized with PE.
questions.priority: Support the child's development during hospitalization.

questions.stem: A client with PE is receiving thrombolytic therapy. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Monitor for epistaxis, hematuria and bruising
Give PRN pain medication by intramuscular injection
Watch the hemoglobin and hematocrit for a drop
Draw each lab by a separate venipuncture
Ensure a safe environment when the client walks
rationales: Correct. The book lists monitoring for bleeding, including epistaxis, hematuria and bruising.
Incorrect. The book says to limit invasive procedures such as injections during therapy.
Correct. An H/H drop is listed as a bleeding sign to monitor.
Incorrect. The book says to limit venipunctures during anticoagulant or thrombolytic therapy.
Correct. The book lists ensuring a safe environment for ambulatory clients.
questions.clue: Client is receiving thrombolytic therapy.
questions.priority: Prevent and detect bleeding during clot-dissolving therapy.

questions.stem: A client with symptomatic PE is receiving a weight-based IV heparin infusion. Which laboratory result does the nurse use to guide adjustment of the infusion?
options: D-dimer level
Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)
Platelet count
Chest x-ray result
rationales: Incorrect. The book uses a positive D-dimer to show there is a clot somewhere, not to adjust heparin.
Correct. The book states the IV heparin bolus and infusion are adjusted by aPTT.
Incorrect. The book does not use the platelet count to adjust the heparin infusion.
Incorrect. A chest x-ray is not used to titrate heparin.
questions.clue: Weight-based heparin infusion for symptomatic PE.
questions.priority: Monitor the correct lab for heparin therapy.

questions.stem: A client is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. Orders include blood cultures, sputum culture, and IV antibiotics. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Start the IV antibiotic infusion
Teach the client incentive spirometry
Obtain an ABG right after suctioning
Collect the blood and sputum cultures
rationales: Incorrect. Giving antibiotics before cultures can prevent identification of the organism.
Incorrect. Incentive spirometry prevents atelectasis but does not come before cultures and antibiotics.
Incorrect. The book warns not to suction before an ABG because it lowers oxygen and skews results.
Correct. The book states to collect cultures first and then start antibiotics early.
questions.clue: Cultures and antibiotics are both ordered on admission.
questions.priority: Identify the organism before starting antibiotic therapy.

questions.stem: A client has pneumonia in the right lung with no hemoptysis or abscess. To improve ventilation-perfusion matching, how should the nurse position the client?
options: Side-lying with the right lung down
Side-lying with the left lung down
Flat supine with the head of bed at zero
Trendelenburg with the legs raised
rationales: Incorrect. Placing the affected lung down sends more blood flow to poorly ventilated tissue.
Correct. The book advises good lung down; the left lung is unaffected here.
Incorrect. Lying flat does not favor the good lung and raises aspiration risk.
Incorrect. Trendelenburg is used after witnessed aspiration, not to improve V/Q matching in pneumonia.
questions.clue: Pneumonia is in the right lung only, with no exceptions present.
questions.priority: Optimize gas exchange through positioning.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for an intubated client on a ventilator. Which action best helps prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia?
options: Change the ventilator circuit on a set daily schedule
Use an open suction technique for each suction pass
Hold daily sedation interruptions to keep comfort
Keep the head of bed at 30 to 45 degrees unless contraindicated
rationales: Incorrect. The book says to avoid routine circuit changes unless visibly soiled.
Incorrect. The book recommends closed in-line suction systems to reduce contamination.
Incorrect. Daily sedation vacations and readiness checks for extubation are part of VAP prevention.
Correct. The book lists head-of-bed elevation of 30 to 45 degrees, unless contraindicated, in VAP prevention.
questions.clue: Client is intubated and on mechanical ventilation.
questions.priority: Prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia.

questions.stem: A client has been intubated and mechanically ventilated for three days. Which measures should the nurse use to prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP)? Select all that apply.
options: Change the ventilator circuit every 24 hours
Provide oral hygiene with chlorhexidine every 12 hours
Use an open suction technique for each pass
Suction subglottic secretions
Assess extubation readiness during daily sedation vacations
Lower the head of the bed flat to promote rest
rationales: Incorrect. The book says to avoid routine ventilator circuit changes unless visibly soiled.
Correct. The book lists oral hygiene with chlorhexidine every 12 hours.
Incorrect. The book recommends closed in-line suction systems to reduce contamination.
Correct. The book lists suctioning of subglottic secretions in intubated clients.
Correct. The book lists daily sedation vacations and assessment of extubation readiness.
Incorrect. The book directs head-of-bed elevation of 30 to 45 degrees unless contraindicated.
questions.clue: Client is intubated and on a ventilator.
questions.priority: Apply the VAP prevention bundle.

questions.stem: A client is admitted with suspected bacterial pneumonia. For each diagnostic result, indicate whether it is normal or abnormal.
rows: Chest x-ray showing an infiltrate in the right lower lobe
Sputum culture showing growth of infecting bacteria
ABG with PaO2 and PaCO2 in the normal range
rationales: The book lists a normal WBC of 4,500 to 11,000/mm3; leukocytosis is abnormal.
An infiltrate or consolidation is the abnormal chest x-ray finding.
Negative blood cultures are the normal result.
Growth of infecting bacteria is the abnormal sputum result.
Normal PaO2 and PaCO2 are the normal ABG result; hypoxemia and hypocapnia are abnormal.
questions.clue: Comparing each result with the book's normal and abnormal values.
questions.priority: Interpret diagnostic results in pneumonia.

questions.stem: The nurse is screening adults at a community clinic. Which client factors are risk factors for pneumonia? Select all that apply.
options: Cigarette smoking
Long-term steroid use
Regular moderate exercise
Alcohol abuse
Taking a daily multivitamin
rationales: Correct. Smoking is shown as a pneumonia risk factor.
Correct. Steroids are shown with HIV and chemotherapy as a risk factor.
Incorrect. Exercise is not a listed risk factor; immobility is.
Correct. Alcohol abuse is shown as a pneumonia risk factor.
Incorrect. A daily multivitamin is not a listed risk factor; malnutrition is.
questions.clue: Exposures and conditions that weaken lung defenses.
questions.priority: Identify clients at risk for pneumonia for prevention teaching.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for four clients with pneumonia. Which client should the nurse see first?
options: A client with a productive cough and a temperature of 38.1 C (100.6 F)
A client asking for help using the incentive spirometer
A client whose blood pressure is 82/48 mm Hg with a heart rate of 128/min
A client with crackles in the right lower lobe noted on admission
rationales: Incorrect. Cough and fever are expected pneumonia findings and are not the most urgent.
Incorrect. Incentive spirometry is important but can wait briefly.
Correct. The book lists septic shock as a complication of pneumonia; hypotension with tachycardia suggests it and needs immediate assessment.
Incorrect. Crackles that have been present since admission are an expected finding, not a new change.
questions.clue: Hypotension and tachycardia in a client with pneumonia.
questions.priority: Recognize a life-threatening complication first.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with suspected pneumonia has a chest x-ray ordered. Which action should the nurse take before the study?
options: Hold the first antibiotic dose until the x-ray is read
Have the client fast for 8 hours
Suction the client to clear the airway
Confirm that a pregnancy test has been done
rationales: Incorrect. The book says to start antibiotics early once cultures are collected; the x-ray does not delay them.
Incorrect. Fasting is not required for a chest x-ray.
Incorrect. Suctioning is not a preparation step for radiography.
Correct. The book states to perform pregnancy tests before radiography studies in all women of childbearing age.
questions.clue: A woman of childbearing age is going for an x-ray.
questions.priority: Prevent fetal radiation exposure.

questions.stem: A client recovering from pneumonia spends most of the day in bed. Which nursing action best helps prevent atelectasis?
options: Encourage turning, coughing, deep breathing and incentive spirometry
Limit position changes to conserve the client's energy
Encourage shallow breathing to reduce chest discomfort
Keep the client flat in bed to rest the lungs
rationales: Correct. The book says to encourage TCDB (turn, cough, deep breathe) and incentive spirometry to prevent atelectasis.
Incorrect. Turning is part of TCDB; limiting it raises the risk of atelectasis.
Incorrect. Shallow breathing promotes atelectasis; the book calls for deep breathing.
Incorrect. Lying flat does not help clear secretions or expand the lungs.
questions.clue: A client with pneumonia is mostly in bed.
questions.priority: Prevent atelectasis through lung expansion.

questions.stem: While being fed, a client suddenly coughs and chokes, and the nurse sees food in the mouth. What should the nurse do immediately?
options: Sit the client fully upright and offer sips of water
Place the client in slight Trendelenburg and suction the mouth and pharynx
Resume the meal at a slower rate with smaller bites
Wait for a chest x-ray before taking any action
rationales: Incorrect. Giving fluids adds more material that can be aspirated; the airway must be cleared first.
Correct. For witnessed aspiration, the book lists slight Trendelenburg and oral and pharyngeal suction.
Incorrect. The book advises NPO until a swallow evaluation clears the client.
Incorrect. Imaging is for monitoring; clearing the airway comes first.
questions.clue: Witnessed choking with food in the mouth during a meal.
questions.priority: Clear the airway right after a witnessed aspiration.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing assigned clients. Which client has the highest risk for aspiration?
options: Alert client walking in the hall after surgery
Client on a regular diet who sits upright for meals
Client with altered consciousness on NG tube feedings lying flat
Alert client with an intact gag reflex awaiting tests
rationales: Incorrect. An alert, mobile client has none of the risk factors the book lists.
Incorrect. Upright positioning is a prevention measure, not a risk factor.
Correct. The book lists altered consciousness, enteral feeding and lying flat during feeding as aspiration risk factors.
Incorrect. An intact gag reflex protects the airway; an absent one is the risk factor.
questions.clue: Altered consciousness plus enteral feeding while lying flat.
questions.priority: Identify clients at greatest aspiration risk.

questions.stem: A client is suspected of aspirating vomit. When reviewing the chest x-ray, where should the nurse expect the aspirated material to be found?
options: In the right lung
In the left lung
Evenly in both lung apices
In the pleural space only
rationales: Correct. The book explains most aspiration enters the right lung because its mainstem bronchus is shorter, wider and less angled.
Incorrect. The left mainstem bronchus is longer and more angled, so it is less often involved.
Incorrect. Gravity and airway anatomy favor the right side, not even spread to the apices.
Incorrect. Aspirated material enters the airways and lungs, not the pleural space.
questions.clue: Suspected aspiration of vomit.
questions.priority: Anticipate the anatomic site of aspiration.

questions.stem: A client with a history of dysphagia had a suspected aspiration event and is now stable. Which prevention measures should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Offer thin liquids at the bedside to test swallowing
Keep the client NPO until cleared
Keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees or higher
Lay the client flat after each tube feeding
Arrange a swallow evaluation
rationales: Incorrect. The book says to keep the client NPO until cleared by a swallow evaluation.
Correct. The book lists NPO until cleared as a prevention measure.
Correct. The book lists HOB at 30 degrees or higher.
Incorrect. The book lists lying flat during or after feeding as a risk factor.
Correct. The book lists a swallow evaluation as a prevention measure.
questions.clue: History of dysphagia and a recent aspiration event.
questions.priority: Prevent repeat aspiration.

questions.stem: The nurse cares for two clients: one choked on food while the nurse watched, and one was found with gastric contents in the oropharynx after an unobserved event. For each intervention, indicate whether the book lists it for witnessed or unwitnessed aspiration.
rows: Suction of the oral cavity and pharynx
Monitoring for pneumonia, ARDS or hypotension
rationales: Slight Trendelenburg is listed for witnessed aspiration.
Oral and pharyngeal suction is listed for witnessed aspiration.
Intubation or mechanical ventilation is listed for unwitnessed aspiration.
Bronchoscopy for large particles is listed for witnessed aspiration.
Monitoring for pneumonia, ARDS or hypotension is listed for unwitnessed aspiration.
questions.clue: Whether the aspiration event was witnessed.
questions.priority: Match interventions to the type of aspiration event.

questions.stem: A client receiving nasogastric tube feedings is found lying flat and coughing. Which findings should the nurse recognize as signs of aspiration? Select all that apply.
options: Crackles on auscultation
Hypoxemia
Bradycardia
Gastric contents in the oropharynx
Tachycardia
Elevated blood pressure
rationales: Correct. Crackles are listed as a sign of aspiration.
Correct. Hypoxemia is listed as a sign of aspiration.
Incorrect. The book lists tachycardia, not bradycardia.
Correct. Gastric contents in the oropharynx are listed as a sign of aspiration.
Correct. Tachycardia is listed as a sign of aspiration.
Incorrect. The book lists hypotension, not high blood pressure.
questions.clue: Tube-fed client lying flat and coughing.
questions.priority: Recognize aspiration early.

questions.stem: A client develops a lung infection after an aspiration event. Blood and sputum cultures have been sent. Which antibiotic plan should the nurse anticipate?
options: Withhold antibiotics until the culture results are final
Start empiric antibiotics and adjust them based on culture results
Give a single antibiotic dose only if a fever develops
Use antibiotics only if bronchoscopy finds large particles
rationales: Incorrect. The book says to start empiric antibiotics, not wait for final results.
Correct. The book's treatment summary says to start empiric antibiotics and adjust per cultures.
Incorrect. A single fever-triggered dose is not the book's plan.
Incorrect. Bronchoscopy removes large particles; it does not decide whether antibiotics are given.
questions.clue: Infection after aspiration with cultures already sent.
questions.priority: Treat infection promptly and tailor therapy to cultures.

questions.stem: A client with COPD is hypoxic during an acute exacerbation. Which oxygen order should the nurse expect?
options: Low-flow oxygen by nasal cannula with a saturation target near 90%
Non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min to reach 100% saturation
No oxygen until arterial blood gas results return
High-flow oxygen with a saturation target of 98%
rationales: Correct. The book calls for low-flow oxygen, about 1 to 2 L by nasal cannula, targeting a saturation near 90%.
Incorrect. High-flow oxygen is avoided in COPD; the book stresses careful low-flow titration.
Incorrect. A hypoxic client needs oxygen; the book says to adjust it carefully, not withhold it.
Incorrect. The book's target for COPD is about 90%, delivered at low flow.
questions.clue: Hypoxic client with COPD.
questions.priority: Provide safe, carefully titrated oxygen in COPD.

questions.stem: A client with chronic COPD who still smokes asks which change will help the disease most. What is the nurse's best response?
options: Taking aminophylline daily will best control symptoms
Long-term corticosteroids are the main treatment
Quitting smoking is the most important step you can take
Using albuterol every few hours will stop progression
rationales: Incorrect. The book advises avoiding aminophylline because of toxicity and interactions.
Incorrect. The book says corticosteroids have a limited role because of side effects.
Correct. The book names smoking cessation as the most important chronic management intervention.
Incorrect. Short-acting albuterol is for rescue use and does not change the disease course.
questions.clue: Client with COPD continues to smoke.
questions.priority: Teach the intervention with the greatest long-term benefit.

questions.stem: A client with a COPD exacerbation is being assessed. Which finding most suggests a bacterial cause?
options: Symptoms that started after pollen exposure
Sputum changing from clear to creamy and purulent
Exertional dyspnea that has slowly increased
Wheezing that started after smoke exposure
rationales: Incorrect. Pollen is an environmental allergen trigger, not a sign of bacterial infection.
Correct. The book lists more sputum and a color change from clear to purulent as signs of bacterial infection.
Incorrect. Exertional dyspnea is a baseline COPD symptom and does not point to bacteria.
Incorrect. Smoke is an airway irritant trigger, not evidence of bacterial infection.
questions.clue: Change in sputum color from clear to purulent.
questions.priority: Recognize signs of a bacterial COPD exacerbation.

questions.stem: A client recently diagnosed with COPD asks why a blood test for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency was ordered. What is the nurse's best response?
options: "It is repeated every year to measure smoking damage."
"It is checked only in people who have never smoked."
"It shows how well your inhaler is working."
"Everyone with COPD is screened once for this genetic factor, which is linked to early-onset COPD."
rationales: Incorrect. The book says to screen once, not yearly.
Incorrect. The book says to screen all clients with COPD.
Incorrect. The test looks for a genetic deficiency, not inhaler effect.

Discharge with no treatment

Correct. The book lists needle aspiration for a primary spontaneous pneumothorax under 20% that is symptomatic.
Incorrect. The book reserves pigtail catheter aspiration with low suction or water seal for pneumothorax over 20%.
Incorrect. A symptomatic client needs treatment; even small pneumothoraces get oxygen and monitoring.
questions.clue: Pneumothorax under 20% with symptoms.
questions.priority: Match treatment to pneumothorax size and symptoms.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with a chest tube after a pneumothorax. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Keep the drainage collection chamber lower than the chest
Coil extra tubing in dependent loops below the bed
Clamp the tube routinely whenever the client walks
Clamp only when changing the system, with a physician order
Avoid high airway pressure to prevent an air leak
rationales: Correct. The book says to keep the collection chamber lower than the chest.
Incorrect. The book says the tubing must have no dependent loops.
Incorrect. The book says to clamp only when changing the system, with a physician order.
Correct. The book states clamping is done only when changing the system with an order.
Correct. The book lists avoiding high airway pressure to prevent air leak.
questions.clue: Client has a chest tube drainage system.
questions.priority: Maintain a safe, functioning chest drainage system.

questions.stem: A client has chest trauma. For each finding, indicate whether the book links it to tension pneumothorax or to spontaneous or traumatic pneumothorax.
rows: Tracheal deviation away from the affected side
Tracheal deviation, if present, toward the affected side
Hypoxemia that occurs if the pneumothorax is large
rationales: Deviation away from the affected side is listed for tension pneumothorax.
Deviation toward the affected side is listed for spontaneous or traumatic pneumothorax.
Distended neck veins and hypotension are listed for tension pneumothorax.
Hypoxemia (if large) is listed for spontaneous or traumatic pneumothorax.
questions.clue: Direction of tracheal shift and hemodynamic signs.
questions.priority: Differentiate a life-threatening tension pneumothorax.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients. Which client should the nurse see first?
options: A client with a chest tube whose drainage chamber is below the chest and tubing has no loops
A client with a small pneumothorax on oxygen who is waiting for a repeat x-ray
A client after a stab wound with distended neck veins, hypotension and a trachea shifted away from the injury
A client asking for PRN pain medicine for chest tube discomfort
rationales: Incorrect. This chest tube is set up correctly per the book.
Incorrect. Oxygen and monitoring for re-expansion is the book's plan for a small pneumothorax; this client is stable.
Correct. These are the book's signs of tension pneumothorax, a life-threatening emergency.
Incorrect. The book lists treating pain as needed, but it is not the most urgent need.
questions.clue: Distended neck veins, hypotension and tracheal shift away from the injury.
questions.priority: See the client with a life-threatening emergency first.

questions.stem: A client with active pulmonary TB is admitted. How long should the nurse maintain airborne isolation?
options: Until the first dose of drug therapy is given
Until three sputum AFB samples are negative
Until the client no longer has a fever
Until one sputum AFB sample is negative
rationales: Incorrect. Starting drugs does not end isolation; negative sputum samples are required.
Correct. The book states airborne isolation continues until three negative AFB sputum samples.
Incorrect. Fever resolving does not show the client is no longer infectious.
Incorrect. The book requires three negative samples, not one.
questions.clue: Client has active pulmonary TB.
questions.priority: Prevent airborne spread of TB.

questions.stem: A client who received the BCG vaccine as a child has a positive TB skin test. What should the nurse expect next?
options: Evaluation with a chest x-ray
Repeating the same skin test
Starting four-drug therapy at once
No further action because of BCG
rationales: Correct. The book states BCG recipients have a positive skin test and should be evaluated by chest x-ray.
Incorrect. A BCG recipient will test positive again, so repeating it adds little.
Incorrect. A positive skin test after BCG needs further evaluation before treatment.
Incorrect. The book directs a chest x-ray rather than ignoring the result.
questions.clue: Positive skin test in a client who received BCG.
questions.priority: Use the correct follow-up test after BCG.

questions.stem: An inpatient with TB is ready to go home on drug therapy. Which action must the nurse ensure before discharge?
options: The client has finished all drug therapy
The health department has been notified
The client has had a repeat BCG vaccine
Family contacts need no further screening
rationales: Incorrect. Therapy lasts 6 to 9 months or longer and continues after discharge.
Correct. The book states the health department must be notified before an inpatient with TB is discharged.
Incorrect. The book does not list BCG as part of discharge or treatment.
Incorrect. The book calls for follow-up of contacts with screening and prophylaxis.
questions.clue: Inpatient with TB is being discharged.
questions.priority: Meet public health reporting requirements for TB.

questions.stem: A client hospitalized with active TB is weak and short of breath. Which supportive nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Position the client upright
Limit food intake to reduce the work of breathing
Encourage deep breathing and coughing
Promote rest and assist with self-care
Keep the client flat to reduce coughing
rationales: Correct. The book lists positioning upright to ensure oxygenation.
Incorrect. The book lists nutrition as part of supporting recovery.
Correct. The book lists deep breathing and coughing to ensure oxygenation.
Correct. The book lists promoting rest and assisting with self-care to support recovery.
Incorrect. The book calls for upright positioning.
questions.clue: Weak, short-of-breath client with active TB.
questions.priority: Support oxygenation and recovery.

questions.stem: A client is starting a TB drug regimen. For each drug, indicate the mechanism the book lists for it.
rationales: The book lists INH as inhibiting mycobacterial cell wall synthesis.
The book lists RIF as blocking RNA synthesis and targeting slow-growing bacilli.
The book lists streptomycin as inhibiting protein synthesis by ribosomal binding.
questions.clue: Each drug's mechanism of action.
questions.priority: Understand how each TB drug works.

questions.stem: The nurse is screening clients at a clinic. Which clients have history findings that increase their risk for TB? Select all that apply.
options: A client with HIV
A nonsmoking office worker with no illnesses who has not traveled
A client who lives in a homeless shelter
A client taking long-term corticosteroids
A teenager with mild seasonal allergies and no known exposures
rationales: Correct. HIV is listed in the medical and exposure history.
Incorrect. None of the book's risk factors are present.
Correct. Homelessness and shelter residence are listed.
Correct. Use of corticosteroids or immunosuppressants is listed.
Incorrect. Seasonal allergies are not a listed risk factor.
questions.clue: Immunosuppression and crowded living conditions.
questions.priority: Identify clients who need TB screening.

questions.stem: A client with active TB who started INH, RIF, PZA and ETB says, "Once my cough is gone in a few weeks, I can stop the pills." What is the nurse's best response?
options: "Yes, you may stop once your symptoms are gone."
"You only need the pills until your skin test turns negative."
"Treatment usually lasts 6 to 9 months, and taking every dose is essential."
"You can stop the pills if you get the BCG vaccine."
rationales: Incorrect. The book gives a standard duration of 6 to 9 months, longer for drug-resistant TB.
Incorrect. Duration is set by the regimen, not by the skin test.
Correct. The book gives a standard duration of 6 to 9 months and states medication adherence is essential.
Incorrect. BCG is not part of TB treatment.
questions.clue: Client plans to stop TB drugs once symptoms improve.
questions.priority: Promote adherence to the full TB regimen.

questions.stem: An inpatient with active TB lives with three family members. Which action reflects coordinated follow-up of these contacts?
options: Arrange screening and prophylaxis for the family contacts
Tell the family no follow-up is needed unless they feel sick
Delay contact follow-up until the client finishes therapy
Offer the family BCG vaccine in place of screening
rationales: Correct. The book calls for follow-up of contacts, ensuring screening and prophylaxis.
Incorrect. The book calls for screening of contacts, not waiting for symptoms.
Incorrect. Therapy lasts months; contacts need follow-up now.
Incorrect. The book directs screening and prophylaxis, not BCG.
questions.clue: Household contacts of a client with active TB.
questions.priority: Coordinate public health follow-up of contacts.

questions.stem: A client's ABG shows pH 7.30, PaCO2 52 mmHg, and HCO3 24 mEq/L. How should the nurse interpret these results?
options: Respiratory acidosis
Respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis
rationales: Correct. The pH is low and PaCO2 is high with normal HCO3, which the book defines as respiratory acidosis.
Incorrect. Respiratory alkalosis has a high pH and a low PaCO2.
Incorrect. Metabolic acidosis shows a low HCO3, but HCO3 here is normal.
Incorrect. Metabolic alkalosis has a high pH and a high HCO3.
questions.clue: Low pH with high PaCO2 and normal HCO3.
questions.priority: Interpret ABGs to guide respiratory care.

questions.stem: A client with COPD needs a precise, controlled amount of oxygen. Which device should the nurse expect to use?
options: Non-rebreather mask
Partial rebreather mask
Venturi mask
Simple face mask
rationales: Incorrect. The non-rebreather gives up to 100% oxygen for emergencies, not precise low levels.
Incorrect. A partial rebreather gives 60 to 80% and is not described as precise.
Correct. The book lists the Venturi mask as giving a precise FiO2 and as best for COPD.
Incorrect. A simple mask is for short-term use and is not described as precise.
questions.clue: COPD client needs a precise FiO2.
questions.priority: Choose the oxygen device that fits the client's needs.

questions.stem: The nurse finds a client's simple face mask running at 3 L/min. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Leave the flow at 3 L/min as set
Lower the flow to 1 L/min
Switch to BVM at 3 L/min
Raise the flow to at least 6 L/min
rationales: Incorrect. A simple mask below 6 L/min is below the minimum the book lists.
Incorrect. Lowering the flow moves further below the required minimum.
Incorrect. A BVM is for emergency manual ventilation at 15 L/min.
Correct. The book states a simple mask must run at 6 L/min or more.
questions.clue: Simple face mask set at 3 L/min.
questions.priority: Deliver oxygen safely and correctly.

questions.stem: For each set of arterial blood gas results, indicate the acid-base imbalance.
rows: pH 7.50, PaCO2 30 mm Hg, HCO3 24 mEq/L
pH 7.31, PaCO2 40 mm Hg, HCO3 18 mEq/L
pH 7.28, PaCO2 55 mm Hg, HCO3 24 mEq/L
pH 7.47, PaCO2 32 mm Hg, HCO3 23 mEq/L
rationales: High pH with low PaCO2 and normal HCO3 is respiratory alkalosis.
Low pH with low HCO3 and normal PaCO2 is metabolic acidosis.
Low pH with high PaCO2 and normal HCO3 is respiratory acidosis.
High pH with low PaCO2 and normal HCO3 is respiratory alkalosis.
questions.clue: Which value, PaCO2 or HCO3, is outside its normal range.
questions.priority: Interpret ABGs using the book's normal ranges.

questions.stem: A charge nurse reviews care plans on a respiratory unit. Which plans match the book's respiratory nursing priorities? Select all that apply.
options: Client with TB: N95 mask and a negative-pressure room
Client with COPD: high-flow oxygen to keep saturation at 100%
Client with emphysema: encourage pursed-lip breathing
Client with pulmonary fibrosis: energy conservation
Client with dyspnea: keep the head of bed flat
Client with TB: report to public health authorities
rationales: Correct. The book lists airborne precautions for TB with an N95 mask and negative-pressure room.
Incorrect. The book calls for low-flow oxygen for COPD and emphysema.
Correct. The book lists pursed-lip breathing for emphysema.
Correct. The book lists conserving energy in pulmonary fibrosis.
Incorrect. The book says to elevate the head of the bed to ease breathing.
Correct. The book lists reporting TB to public health.
questions.clue: Each plan compared with the book's priority list.
questions.priority: Apply respiratory nursing priorities across clients.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews respiratory rates for four clients. Which client needs follow-up first?
options: An infant breathing 44 breaths/min
A 7-year-old breathing 24 breaths/min
An adult breathing 16 breaths/min
An adult breathing 28 breaths/min
rationales: Incorrect. The book gives 30 to 60 breaths/min as normal for an infant.
Incorrect. The book gives 20 to 30 breaths/min as normal for a child.
Incorrect. The book gives 12 to 20 breaths/min as normal for an adult.
Correct. An adult rate of 28 is above the book's normal range of 12 to 20 breaths/min.
questions.clue: Only one rate is outside its age-specific normal range.
questions.priority: Use age-specific norms to set priorities.

questions.stem: A client is receiving oxygen by non-rebreather mask, and the reservoir bag collapses completely with each breath. What should the nurse do?
options: Increase the flow, within 10 to 15 L/min, so the bag stays inflated
Remove the reservoir bag from the mask
Switch to a nasal cannula at 6 L/min
Lower the flow to 6 L/min
rationales: Correct. The book lists a non-rebreather at 10 to 15 L/min and says to keep the bag inflated.
Incorrect. The reservoir bag must stay inflated to deliver high oxygen.
Incorrect. A nasal cannula gives only 24 to 44% and is for mild hypoxia, not emergency oxygen.
Incorrect. 6 L/min is below the book's 10 to 15 L/min range for a non-rebreather.
questions.clue: Non-rebreather bag collapses with each breath.
questions.priority: Use oxygen equipment correctly.

concerns.issue: States patients 'tend to tolerate a pH <7.2' with rising PaCO2, which contradicts page 16 ('Permissive hypercapnia acceptable if pH > 7.2').
'PEEP usually 15 cm H2O or greater' is stated as a general rule for ARDS; this is an overgeneralization since PEEP is titrated (as page 16 itself says).
Typo 'surface tention'; also the PEEP rationale claims PEEP decreases surface tension, which is not its mechanism (surfactant affects surface tension; PEEP keeps alveoli open).

Physiology statement says the brainstem detects low PaO2 and peripheral regulation occurs in the aortic arch only; central chemoreceptors respond mainly to CO2/pH, and the carotid bodies (main peripheral oxygen sensors) are omitted.
'Low PaCO2 is the primary drive for breathing for these patients' is incorrect; it should be low PaO2 (hypoxic drive), and it contradicts page 15.
Typos: 'FEV,/FVC' should be FEV1/FVC; 'a-1 antitrypsindeficiency' missing space; 'Corticosteroids Antibiotics (if increased mucus production)' runs two items together.
Warfarin target INR listed as 2.5-3.5 for PE/VTE; the usual VTE target is 2.0-3.0.

Pneumonia definition: 'micromutant' appears to be a typo for microorganism; 'lung interstitial' should be interstitium; 'lobular pneumonia' for part of a lobe and 'lobar pneumonia' for an entire lung are mislabeled (lobar pneumonia involves a lobe).
Diagnosis table lists 'Egophony or fluid collection' as the abnormal thoracentesis fluid result; egophony is an auscultation finding, not a fluid result. Also 'Bloud Gases' typo.
Pulmonary embolism section has no 'A2. Pulmonary embolism' heading; the section starts directly with Table 2.
Section numbering is inconsistent: Asthma (p27), Emphysema (p32) and Pulmonary Fibrosis (p34) lack A6/A8/A9 labels while other sections are numbered.

Asthma classification thresholds overlap or are inconsistent (mild intermittent '<2x/week' vs mild persistent '2x/week'); 'percusion' and 'suprac-clavicular' typos; vocal fremitus listed among asthma signs is questionable.
Status asthmaticus diagnostic table repeats the 'Fatigue/Lethargy/Confusion' row twice.

The Remember box in the pleural effusion section (avoid high O2 flow, monitor for respiratory acidosis, small high-calorie meals, vaccines) is identical to the emphysema box on page 34 and appears misplaced for pleural effusion.
'Four Types of Emphysema' lists bronchiectasis as an emphysema type; bronchiectasis is a separate airway disease, not a type of emphysema.
Pulmonary fibrosis PFTs listed as small airway obstruction and increased residual volume (air trapping), which contradicts the page 34 description of fibrosis as a restrictive disease.
Pneumothorax infographic is titled 'Two Types of Pneumothorax' while page 36 states there are three primary forms.
Venturi mask row places '24-60%' (an FiO2 value) in the Flow column instead of a flow rate.
Typos in cheat sheet: 'pneumoia' in auscultation sounds; 'confussion' on page 38 TB assessment.

'Avoid triggers (allergens, cold, exercise, NSAIDs)' tells clients with asthma to avoid exercise, which conflicts with the same page's use of albuterol before exercise; exercise is usually pre-treated rather than avoided.
Level-of-care thresholds 'PFR < 50% admit to ICU / PFR > 50 -70% admit to telemetry' use unclear notation and are not a widely standardized rule.
'Increase I/E 1:3-4' / 'Increase I/E ratio to prevent auto-PEEP' is ambiguous; the intent is to lengthen expiratory time (I:E 1:3 to 1:4). Not used as a keyed item.
Emphysema risk factor 'Substance use (e.g. cocaine, IV methadone(methylphenidate))' is garbled; IV methylphenidate use is the recognized association.
Independent nursing actions infographic repeats 'Educate on disease, lifestyle changes, and avoiding irritants' twice; 'occupational/role loss Suicide risk' runs two items together.

Drug mechanisms table describes ethambutol as 'inhibits bacterial metabolite production' and PZA as 'bacteriostatic/cidal; disrupts cell metabolism', which are vague or imprecise (ethambutol inhibits cell wall arabinogalactan synthesis). ETB and PZA mechanisms were not used in items.

ABG interpretation table shows compensatory arrows (e.g., HCO3 up in respiratory acidosis, PaCO2 down in metabolic acidosis) without labeling them as compensation, which can confuse students; items use uncompensated values.
ABG box lists 'PaO2 < 80 mm Hg, SaO2 < 95%' as ARDS diagnostic values; these are nonspecific, and ARDS hypoxemia is defined by the PaO2/FiO2 ratio (page 17).

blueprint: resp chapter has 8 psych (target 9) and 8 bcc (target 9) items; psychosocial and basic-care content in this chapter is limited, so rrp (13) and pa (14) are one over target. All within validator tolerance.
